summary.text: The polynomial remainder theorem, also called little Bézout's theorem, says that dividing a polynomial f(x) by x − r leaves f(r) as the remainder.
As a result, x − r divides f(x) exactly when f(r) = 0, a property known as the factor theorem.
Because synthetic division is computationally easier, the function can be evaluated more cheaply by finding that remainder.

facts.value: Little Bézout's theorem, after Étienne Bézout

facts.value: Dividing by x − 3 leaves remainder −123, so f(3) = −123

facts.label: Factor theorem
facts.value: x − r divides f(x) exactly when f(r) = 0

facts.value: The quotient has degree one less than f

paragraphs.heading: What the theorem says
paragraphs.text: The polynomial remainder theorem, also called little Bézout's theorem after Étienne Bézout, grows out of dividing one polynomial by another with a remainder. Pick any number r. The theorem says any polynomial f(x) equals f(r) plus a product: x − r times another polynomial in x. That other polynomial has a degree one lower than f.

paragraphs.heading: The remainder is a value
paragraphs.text: Put another way, when you divide f(x) by x − r, the remainder is simply f(r), the value you get by plugging r into the polynomial. It follows that x − r divides f(x) with nothing left over exactly when f(r) = 0. That special case has its own name, the factor theorem.

paragraphs.heading: A worked case
paragraphs.text: Suppose some polynomial f(x) is divided by (x − 3), and the work yields x² − 9x − 27 as the quotient with −123 left over. The theorem then tells you, with no further work, that f(3) = −123.

paragraphs.heading: Why it holds
paragraphs.text: In one worked case, the algebra rearranges into f(x) = (x − r)(ax + ar + b) + f(r). That is exactly the shape of division with a remainder, with f(r) sitting in the remainder's place. The same proof extends to polynomials of every degree. In this case it also shows, at the same time, that such a division exists.

paragraphs.heading: A cheaper way to evaluate
paragraphs.text: Because the remainder equals f(r), you can find the value f(r) by working out the remainder R. Doing that with polynomial long division would be harder than just plugging r in. Synthetic division, however, is easier on the arithmetic. So pairing synthetic division with this theorem can be a more economical way to evaluate a polynomial.

paragraphs.heading: Factoring step by step
paragraphs.text: The factor theorem is another application of this result. If dividing by a linear divisor such as x − r leaves zero, that divisor is a factor of the polynomial. Applying this test again and again, one factor at a time, lets you break a polynomial down into its factors.
